svg.title: The shared invalidation queue in five steps
svg.desc: Five steps on one ring of 4096 queue slots. 1, write: a session creates and drops a temp table, which puts 132 invalidation messages into the queue, 71 for CREATE and 61 for DROP. 2, read: an active session reads the new messages at its next transaction start; an idle session does not read, so the unread part of the ring grows behind it. 3, catch up: in transaction 16 the queue is more than half full, 2048 messages; the writer signals the session that is furthest behind, which wakes up, reads its backlog and takes the lock SInvalWrite to pass the signal on. 4, lapped: a session that is busy in a long statement does not act on the signal; 31 transactions fill the queue, transaction 32 laps the session, and it must reset all its caches. 5, at scale: with 5000 idle sessions only one is signalled at a time, the writer laps most of the others, and the writers wait for the lock. Measured on Postgres 18.6 with 16 writers at a target of 500 TPS, for 0, 1000, 3000 and 5000 idle sessions: 502, 502, 274 and 127 temp-table TPS; LWLock:SInvalWrite 1.3%, 54%, 86% and 91% of the writers' active time; 0.1, 49, 194 and 457 full cache resets per second.
svg.text: 1. A session creates and drops a temp
table. That puts 132 invalidation
messages into the queue.
Each message tells all other sessions to drop one
cached catalog row or table descriptor: 71 for
CREATE, 61 for DROP. The queue is one ring of
4096 slots for the whole Postgres instance. The
writer appends in batches of up to 64 messages
(one cell of the ring) and holds the lock SInvalWrite
for each batch.
2. An active session reads the new
messages at its next transaction start.
An idle session does not read.
Every session has its own read position and must
read every message, 32 at a time. A slot is free
again only after all sessions have read it, so the
idle session holds the queue back. (An active
session also reads when it locks a table.)
3. The queue passes half full, 2048 of
4096 slots: the writer signals the
session that is furthest behind. The idle
session wakes up and reads its
backlog.
This happens in transaction 16. When the idle
session has caught up, it takes the lock SInvalWrite
itself, to pass the signal to the next session that is
behind. One signal at a time, and while a reader
holds the lock, the writers wait.
4. A session that does not read in time
is lapped. This one is in a long
statement and does not act on the
signal: the writer comes around, laps it,
and it must reset its caches.
31 transactions fit. Transaction 32 needs slots that
the session has not read, so its unread messages
are dropped. It cannot know what it missed: at its
next read it throws away all its cached catalog
rows, table descriptors and plans, and loads them
again.
5. With thousands of idle sessions, only
one is signalled at a time. The writer
comes around to the others before their
turn: they are lapped.
A lapped session resets its caches at its next read.
A woken session reads, then takes SInvalWrite and
scans all sessions to pass the signal on. The
writers need the same lock, so they wait. With 5000
idle sessions, temp-table DDL got 127 of the 500
TPS target (249 in a second run).
Measured on Postgres 18.6, 16 writers (step 5 draws
one):

Temp-table TPS

Mechanism: sinvaladt.c. Counts in steps 1 to 4:
Postgres 18.6, table (id int, v text). In step 5 the number
of lapped marks is a sketch, not a measurement. A
lapped session reads again at its next query (one every
30 s in this test), or when a signal that was already sent
reaches it.
